extracted.intended_audience: A.G. Sulzberger (NYT leadership), New York Times staff, and the paper's readership/general public
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion/resignation letter addressed to the publisher describing perceived failures in newsroom culture and journalistic standards, arguing for principles the paper should uphold. It blends personal testimony with normative claims about editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify the voices published
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring in voices that would not otherwise appear in the paper's pages: first-time writers, centrists, conservatives and others who would not naturally think of The Times as their home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites being hired to help redress a failure to grasp the country (post-2016) and lists examples of contributors she helped bring in (e.g., Wuilly Arteaga, Dorsa Derakhshani, Derek Lam, Ayaan Hirsi Ali, Masih Alinejad, Monica Lewinsky, Jesse Singal, Wesley Yang, etc.) as evidence of this work. Anti-pattern: publishing only voices aligned with an internal orthodoxy and excluding perspectives perceived as outside the paper's usual milieu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the country and its diverse audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage should demonstrate a firm grasp of the country it covers and the lives and concerns of most people, not be removed into an intellectual galaxy detached from everyday realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The failure to anticipate the 2016 election is given as an example of lacking understanding. Anti-pattern: producing work that lauds obscure points (e.g., praising the Soviet space program for 'diversity') or treating distant concerns as the paper's central record while neglecting mainstream readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist tribalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism must resist tribalism and avoid treating truth as an orthodoxy known to an enlightened few rather than the result of collective inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that a 'new consensus' treats truth as pre-known and that tribalism leads to selective scrutiny and exclusion. Anti-pattern: applying different standards depending on ideological alignment; 'digital thunderdome' behavior in internal forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect the free exchange of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The free exchange of ideas is central to a democratic society and should be preserved in editorial practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper should invite 'intelligent discussion from all shades of opinion' (Adolph Ochs quote). Anti-pattern: self-censorship, ideological massaging of pieces, and steering writers away from challenging topics to avoid backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let social media (Twitter) become the ultimate editor
rubrics_metrics.description: "Twitter is not on the masthead of The New York Times. But Twitter has become its ultimate editor." Editorial decisions should not be driven by the dynamics of social media mobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editors avoid or sanitize pieces because they are 'likely to inspire backlash internally or on social media', the public is deprived of robust debate. Anti-patterns include choosing stories to satisfy narrow online audiences, massaging language to placate social-media-driven outrage, and excusing online venom when directed at approved targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists should write an accurate, durable record (the 'first rough draft of history')
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are charged with writing the first rough draft of history; coverage should aim for accuracy rather than molding history to fit predetermined narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that history is being 'molded to fit the needs of a predetermined narrative.' Anti-pattern: producing ephemeral accounts aligned to narratives rather than striving for lasting, rigorous reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage intellectual curiosity and risk-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual curiosity and willingness to take editorial or journalistic risks should be rewarded, not treated as liabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter laments that risk-taking is now a liability and that writers/editors avoid challenging work in favor of 'job security (and clicks)'. Anti-pattern: discouraging or penalizing novel or challenging ideas; steering contributors to 'safer ground'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply editorial rules and standards consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing rules and editorial standards must be applied evenly irrespective of the writer's or subject's ideological alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes examples of selective enforcement: the Tom Cotton op-ed was said to have 'fell short of our standards' only after two days and staff changes, while other pieces with problematic content (e.g., Cheryl Strayed's interview with Alice Walker) did not receive similar appended notes. Anti-pattern: selective scrutiny where favored ideological positions escape consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect employees from harassment and hostile work environments
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization must address unlawful discrimination, hostile work environment, and harassment by colleagues, including public smear campaigns on Twitter and internal harassment on platforms like Slack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes being called a Nazi and racist, coworkers badgered, and masthead editors weighing in on Slack with hostile commentary. She references terms like 'unlawful discrimination' and 'constructive discharge.' Anti-pattern: allowing public smears and internal harassment to continue without appropriate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not tolerate self-censorship driven by fear of internal or public backlash
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial culture should not incentivize writers or editors to avoid pitching or publishing work because of fear of backlash; doing so undermines the paper's mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter explains that if a piece is perceived likely to inspire backlash, it is avoided or heavily massaged; editors/writers are 'steered to safer ground.' Anti-pattern: a culture where 'Rule One: Speak your mind at your own peril' is effectively enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve language and standards of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is the 'coin of our realm' and should not be degraded in service of shifting ideological causes; clarity and precision in language must be upheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against degrading language to fit 'an ever-shifting laundry list of right causes.' Anti-pattern: allowing imprecise or ideologically loaded language to supplant rigorous expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain editorial independence from internal 'mobs' and protect editors who commission challenging work
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors who commission or support work that goes against prevailing narratives should be supported rather than reassigned or fired due to mob pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes a pattern where 'the publisher will cave to the mob, the editor will get fired or reassigned, and you'll be hung out to dry.' Anti-pattern: punishing editors for backing controversial yet journalistically defensible pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the paper a forum for all questions of public importance
rubrics_metrics.description: In line with Adolph Ochs's principle, the paper should be a forum inviting consideration and intelligent discussion from all shades of opinion on matters of public importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites Ochs's 1896 statement and emphasizes that ideas need a voice and a hearing backed by people willing to live by them. Anti-pattern: narrowing the forum to only those views that pass a contemporary internal orthodoxy.
